title: Úbeda, 1591
hookLine: dying, he asked to hear the Song of Songs, not the prayers for the dying

lines: A PRIOR WHO DOESN'T LIKE HIM.
cards: By 1591, John of the Cross has lost almost everything the world counts. The leaders of the reform he helped start have turned against him in a quarrel over how it should be run.
He's stripped of every office and sent to a remote friary in the south. Then he gets sick: a fever, and an infection in his leg that won't heal. He needs a town with doctors.
The story goes that he could have gone to a friary where he was loved, and chose Úbeda, where he wasn't known. The prior there doesn't like him.

teach.b: First, the prior. The man in charge at Úbeda resented John and for weeks treated him coldly, complaining about the cost of his care and giving him one of the poorest cells. John didn't fight back.
The story told about the prior is that he later wept and changed his mind about John.
Second, the sores. The infection spread. The doctors cut into his leg again and again, without anything like a modern painkiller.
The friars who nursed him remembered that he hardly complained, and thanked everyone who helped him. Third, the last night. On December 13, he kept asking what time it was.
When they told him it was almost midnight, the story goes, he said he would soon go to sing the morning prayers in heaven. The friars began to read the Church's prayers for the dying.
John stopped them, gently, and asked instead for the Song of Songs, the love poetry of the Bible. They read it to him, and he said: what precious pearls. Fourth, the song.
The accounts don't say exactly which lines.
Here are some from that book, in the Douay-Rheims: "Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone."
A man who'd written so much about dark nights, dying in a cold cell, asking to hear about spring. He died just after midnight, on December 14, 1591. The Church keeps his feast on that day.
For him, it seems, death wasn't a final night.

teach.h: ARISE, MAKE HASTE, MY LOVE, AND COME.
teach.b: It was the Beloved saying: arise, and come.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John of the Cross on December 14, the day he died in Úbeda, and the Church's prayers for the dying are still read at deathbeds, sometimes alongside readings a person has asked for.

games.q: what's inside the last days — tap the pairs.

s: John died honored and at the head of his order
he'd been stripped of every office and was cared for by a prior who resented him.
he asked for the Song of Songs instead of the prayers for the dying
and called the verses precious pearls.
John chose a friary where he was well known and loved
he chose Úbeda, where he wasn't known and the prior disliked him.

games.q: you're John, dying just before midnight. the friars start to read the Church's prayers for the dying. what do you ask for?
o: that they keep going to the end.
that they read the Song of Songs instead.
that they leave you alone in silence.
games.why: he asked for the Song of Songs, the Bible's love poetry, and said: what precious pearls.

practice: Find Song of Songs 2:10 to 13 if you have a Bible nearby, or simply recall those lines about winter being past. Think of a winter in your own life that's ending, or that you hope will end.
If you pray, hear the words as God's to you; if you don't, let them be about spring.

wordCard.voice: Úbeda. The Andalusian town where John of the Cross died, just after midnight on December 14, 1591, asking to hear the Song of Songs. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: arise and come. A man of dark nights, asking for spring. See you tomorrow.
